cards.headline: When someone asks how you are
Choosing a greeting by time of day
cards.note: Buongiorno is for morning and early afternoon. Buonasera starts around 3 or 4 p.m. and lasts the rest of the day, even at 9 p.m. Buonanotte is only for when someone is going to bed.

cards.headline: Asking how someone is
cards.note: Use Lei with a shopkeeper or an older person, and tu with a friend. When you're unsure, use Lei until they offer tu.

rows.text: Mi chiamo Kate. E Lei, come si chiama?
rows.en: My name's Kate. And what's your name?
Nice to meet you. My name's Rosa.

cards.headline: Formal and informal
cards.note: Use Lei with someone you don't know well, and tu with a friend.

cards.headline: When you say where you're from
cards.note: Where you come from starts with sono.

cards.headline: When you say where you live
cards.note: Where you live now starts with abito: abito qui. Where you come from starts with sono.

cards.headline: When you don't understand

rows.text: Può ripetere più piano, per favore?
rows.en: Could you say that again more slowly, please?

cards.note: Non ho capito says you didn't get it, and può ripetere asks them to say it again. Add più piano when you want it slower.

cards.headline: Culture
cards.note: Asking someone to speak more slowly, with più piano, per favore, is perfectly normal. Most people are pleased that you're trying to speak Italian.

cards.headline: When you're asked how long you've been here

rows.text: Da quanto tempo è in Italia?
rows.en: How long have you been in Italy?

rows.text: Sono in Italia da tre settimane.
rows.en: I've been in Italy for three weeks.
How long have you lived here?
I've lived here for a month.

cards.headline: A small word: da

rows.text: Sono in Italia da tre settimane.
rows.en: I've been in Italy for three weeks.
I've lived here for a month.

cards.note: Verb, then da and the time. The time is still going, so Italian keeps the verb in the present.

cards.headline: When you've understood
cards.note: Ho capito means you got it, about something just said.

cards.headline: Formal and informal
cards.note: Use hai capito? with a friend.

cards.headline: When you hear a word you don't know
cards.note: Cosa vuol dire is a ready-made question for a word you heard. Say it just like this and add the word.

cards.headline: When you need a word in Italian

rows.en: How do you say “receipt” in Italian?

cards.note: Come si dice is a ready-made question for a word you need. Say it just like this and add the word.

cards.headline: When you order a drink

rows.en: Good morning! What are you having?
I'll have a sparkling water, thanks.

cards.note: Start with vorrei, I'd like, or prendo, I'll have, then add what you want. When someone asks cosa prende?, prendo is the natural answer.

cards.headline: Culture
cards.note: Cappuccino is a morning drink. After lunch, Italians order an espresso instead.

cards.headline: Ordering one or two

rows.text: Un cappuccino e un cornetto, per favore.
rows.en: A cappuccino and a croissant, please.

rows.text: Una spremuta e due caffè, per favore.
rows.en: A fresh juice and two espressos, please.
So, two pizzas and an orange soda.

cards.note: For one, use un or una (un' before a vowel). For two, say due and change -o to -i and -a to -e. Caffè stays the same.

cards.headline: When you ask the price of one thing
cards.note: For one thing, say quanto costa and then the thing. The answer often starts the same way: costa.

cards.headline: When you ask the price of several things
cards.note: For several things, say quanto costano and then the things. The answer often starts the same way: costano.

cards.headline: What you need at an office

rows.en: You have to take a ticket.

rows.text: Serve una marca da bollo da sedici euro.
rows.en: You need a sixteen-euro revenue stamp.

cards.note: Bisogna goes with a verb and never changes. Serve goes with one thing you need, servono with more than one.

cards.headline: Culture
cards.note: Italian offices often want an appointment booked online. They may also want a marca da bollo, a revenue stamp, bought beforehand at a tabaccheria.

rows.text: Quanto costano un caffè e un cornetto?
rows.en: How much for an espresso and a croissant?

cards.headline: How a price is said
cards.note: Say the euros, then e and the cents: quattro e cinquanta is 4.50. Euro stays the same for any amount. Before uno and otto, the tens lose their last letter: ventotto, trentuno.

cards.headline: A small word: basta

rows.text: Per il contratto basta la fotocopia?
rows.en: For the lease, is a photocopy enough?

rows.text: E di fototessere ne bastano due.
rows.en: And two passport photos are enough.

cards.note: Basta says something is enough. It becomes bastano when what follows is plural.

cards.headline: When you ask how long it takes

rows.text: Di solito ci vogliono quarantacinque giorni.

cards.note: Ci vuole says what something takes. It becomes ci vogliono when what follows is plural, like settimane or giorni.

cards.headline: Asking how you can pay

rows.en: Can I pay with my debit card?

cards.note: Posso pagare asks if you can pay. Then you add how: con la carta, in contanti or con il bancomat.

cards.headline: When you want to pay cash

rows.text: Certo, può pagare in contanti, nessun problema.
rows.en: Sure, you can pay cash, no problem.

cards.note: The answer you hear back is può pagare: you can pay.

cards.headline: Which one, which ones

rows.en: Which form do I need to fill out?
Excuse me, which one do I fill out?

cards.note: Quale asks which one and quali asks which ones, because it agrees with what you're asking about.

cards.headline: How come, how long, how much

rows.text: Quanto costa il corso al mese?
rows.en: How much is the course per month?

cards.note: Come mai asks how come. Quanto asks how much or how long, as in quanto costa and quanto dura.

cards.headline: When a clerk tells you what to do
How polite instructions end

rows.text: Torni con la ricevuta fra trenta giorni.
rows.en: Come back with the receipt in thirty days.

cards.note: A polite instruction ends in -i for -are verbs and in -a for -ere and -ire verbs. So a clerk's firmi means "please sign."

cards.headline: A small word

rows.text: Il conto che ho aperto è gratuito.
rows.en: The account I opened is free.

rows.text: Allora, prendi il bilocale che abbiamo visto ieri?
rows.en: So, are you taking the one-bedroom we saw yesterday?

rows.text: L'idraulico che chiamo di solito è in ferie.
rows.en: The plumber I usually call is on vacation.

cards.note: It links a person or thing to what you say about it. Italian always says che, even where English drops "that."

cards.headline: When you say which one

rows.text: Il bancomat ti ha mangiato la carta.
Quella che mi ha dato la banca la settimana scorsa.
rows.en: The one the bank gave me last week.

cards.note: Che lets you point out the exact one by describing it.

cards.headline: A small word

rows.text: La persona con cui ho parlato ieri oggi non c'è.
rows.en: The person I talked to yesterday isn't here today.

rows.text: Ecco, è questo il documento di cui ho bisogno.
rows.en: There, this is the document I need.

cards.note: Cui says which one you mean after a little word like con, di or in. The little word comes first, then cui, because a sentence never ends on con, di or in.

cards.headline: Two ways to say the place

rows.text: La zona in cui vorrei vivere.
rows.en: The area I'd like to live in.
The area where I'd like to live.

rows.text: La ritira dove ha aperto il conto.
rows.en: You pick it up where you opened your account.

cards.note: When the one you mean is a place, in cui and dove both work.

cards.headline: Saying “what” as “the thing that”:

rows.text: Non capisco bene quello che c'è scritto qui.
rows.en: I don't really understand what it says here.

rows.text: Mi dica pure quello che non è chiaro.
rows.en: Just tell me what isn't clear.
It's just what I was looking for.

cards.note: When “what” means “the thing that,” Italian says quello che. The word che on its own can't stand for the thing.

cards.headline: Formal and informal

rows.text: Quello che conta è la firma.
rows.en: What matters is the signature. · everyday

rows.text: Ciò che conta è la firma.
rows.en: What matters is the signature. · more formal

cards.note: Ciò che says the same as quello che, but it sounds more formal.

cards.headline: Comparing two things

rows.en: This one's brighter than the other one.

rows.text: Il treno è più veloce del pullman.
rows.en: The train is faster than the bus.

cards.note: Più plus di compares two things: più veloce del pullman means faster than the bus.

cards.headline: Picking the best of a group

rows.text: È l'albergo più tranquillo della zona.
rows.en: It's the quietest hotel in the area.

rows.text: Prendo questo: è il più luminoso dei tre.
rows.en: I'm taking this one. It's the brightest of the three.

rows.text: Allora secondo me è il migliore.
rows.en: Then I think it's the best one.

cards.note: Put il or la before più to pick the top one of a group. Il migliore already means "the best."

cards.headline: When you want to know what's allowed

rows.en: Excuse me, is it okay to go in?

rows.text: Sì, ma non si può usare il flash.
rows.en: Yes, but you can't use the flash.

cards.headline: Si può or si possono

rows.en: Can you take pictures of the frescoes?

cards.note: Si può with a verb asks what anyone may do. With a plural, like foto or affreschi, it becomes si possono, because the verb matches the plural.

cards.headline: How long, with da

rows.en: How long have you been studying Italian?
I've been studying Italian for two years.

rows.text: Vivo in Italia da due anni.
rows.en: I've been living in Italy for two years.

cards.note: If something started in the past and is still going on, Italian uses the present, because it isn't over.

cards.headline: How long, with sono … che

rows.text: Sono due anni che vivo qui.
rows.en: I've been living here for two years.

rows.text: Sono già due settimane che aspetto l'idraulico.
rows.en: I've been waiting for the plumber for two weeks already.

rows.text: È un mese che il citofono non funziona.
rows.en: The buzzer hasn't worked in a month.

cards.note: Same meaning as da, with the time first and the verb in the present. With one week or one month, it's è, not sono.

cards.headline: Saying "it to you"

rows.text: La torta? Te la porto stasera.
rows.en: The cake? I'll bring it over tonight.

rows.text: Il trapano? Te lo presto volentieri.
rows.en: The drill? Happy to lend it to you.

rows.text: Le chiavi? Te le restituisco stasera.
rows.en: The keys? I'll give them back to you tonight.

cards.note: Mi and ti become me and te, then lo, la, li or le follows, matching the thing: la for the cake, lo for the drill, le for the keys.

cards.headline: When you want a gift wrapped

rows.en: Could you wrap it for me, please?

cards.note: In almost any shop you can say "È un regalo" and they'll gift-wrap it for free.

cards.headline: When you offer to do it for someone

rows.en: I'll wrap it for you right away.
If you like, I'll bring it to you tonight.

cards.note: Gli, le and Le all become glie- before lo, la, li or le, so glielo can mean it to him, to her or to you.

cards.headline: Offering with posso

rows.en: I can order it for you. · before the verb
I can order it for you. · joined to the verb
I can read it to you, if you'd like.

cards.note: With posso, glielo can go before the verb, or join the end of the infinitive as one word. Both are natural.

cards.headline: When you ask for more at a shop

rows.text: Me ne dà un pezzetto da assaggiare?
rows.en: Could I have a little piece to taste?
Do you like it? Would you like some more?

rows.text: È buonissimo. Me ne dà ancora un etto?
rows.en: It's delicious. Could I have another hundred grams?

cards.headline: A small word

rows.text: Me ne dà ancora due fette?
rows.en: Could I have two more slices?

rows.text: Te ne porto sei, se vuoi.
rows.en: I'll bring you six, if you want.

cards.note: Ne means "of it" or "of them". It joins like lo, so mi becomes me. With an amount, ne is always there, because the amount is of something.

cards.headline: When you forgot something

rows.en: Sorry, I forgot all about it!

rows.text: Il pane? Me ne sono dimenticata anch'io.
rows.en: The bread? I forgot about it too.

rows.text: La bolletta? Me ne dimentico sempre.
rows.en: The bill? I always forget about it.

cards.note: Me ne means "about it" and comes before the verb. In the past, a woman says dimenticata, as in the second line.

cards.headline: Me ne, te ne, se ne

rows.en: No, he forgot all about it.

cards.note: Ne stands for "about it," so me ne, te ne and se ne come before the verb, even where English has nothing.

cards.headline: When you welcome someone you call Lei
cards.note: With Lei, si goes before the verb: si sieda, si accomodi. Prego in front turns the command into a polite invitation.

cards.headline: A small word

rows.en: Go ahead and give me your bag.

cards.note: After a verb, pure means "go ahead," not "also." It makes a command sound like a friendly invitation.

cards.headline: Telling someone what to do, or not

rows.text: Prenda il primo autobus che passa.
rows.en: Take the first bus that comes.

rows.text: Non prenda il 40, oggi non passa.
rows.en: Don't take the 40, it's not running today.

rows.text: Non si preoccupi, Le tengo io il posto.
rows.en: Don't worry, I'll save your seat.

cards.note: With Lei, verbs not ending in -are take -a: prenda. To say don't, just put non in front: non prenda.

cards.headline: When you give directions to someone you call Lei

rows.text: Giri alla prima a destra, per favore.
Vada sempre dritto, poi giri a destra.
rows.en: Go straight ahead, then turn right.

rows.text: Giri alla seconda a sinistra, per favore.

cards.note: With Lei, verbs ending in -are take -i: giri. Andare becomes vada.

cards.headline: A small word

rows.en: I usually wait a few minutes.

cards.note: Qualche means "a few" or "some", but it always takes a singular noun: qualche minuto.

cards.headline: A small phrase
cards.note: Qualcosa di plus a describing word means "something" of that kind.

cards.headline: Set the scene, then say what happened

rows.text: Stavo cucinando quando è saltata la luce.
rows.en: I was cooking when the power went out.

rows.text: Leggevo a letto quando è suonato il telefono.
rows.en: I was reading in bed when the phone rang.

rows.text: Pioveva forte quando siamo usciti dal museo.
rows.en: It was pouring when we came out of the museum.

cards.note: The scene is in the imperfect: stavo cucinando, leggevo, pioveva. What happened is in the passato prossimo: è saltata, è suonato, siamo usciti. It's one event at one moment.

cards.headline: When you're asked what you were doing

rows.text: Ieri sera è saltata la luce. Tu cosa facevi?
rows.en: The power went out last night. What were you doing?

rows.text: Stavo guardando un film quando è saltata la luce.
rows.en: I was watching a movie when the power went out.

cards.headline: When you say what you do

rows.en: What do you do for a living?

cards.note: With sono there is no word for "a": sono ingegnere. Lavoro come works too.

cards.headline: When you talk about your field

rows.en: What field are you in? · informal

rows.text: E Lei, di cosa si occupa?
rows.en: And what do you do? · formal

cards.note: Mi occupo di is for naming the field you work in.

cards.headline: Reason first or reason after

rows.text: Siccome pioveva, abbiamo preso un taxi.
rows.en: Since it was raining, we took a taxi.

rows.text: Abbiamo preso un taxi perché pioveva.
rows.en: We took a taxi because it was raining.

cards.note: Siccome puts the reason first. Perché puts it after what happened. It's the same story told in either order.

cards.headline: A small word

rows.text: Ormai era tardi, quindi ho cenato con pane e formaggio.
rows.en: It was late, so I had bread and cheese.

rows.text: C'era sciopero, quindi ho preso il pullman.
rows.en: There was a strike, so I took the bus.

cards.note: It brings in the result of what you just said: so.

cards.headline: A small word

rows.text: Quando siamo arrivati, il treno era già partito.
rows.en: When we got there, the train had already left.

rows.text: Quando è saltata la luce, avevo già cenato.
rows.en: When the power went out, I'd already had dinner.

cards.note: Già sits before the participle to say something had already happened first. Essere and avere work just as in the passato prossimo.

cards.headline: When it's the first time

rows.text: Non avevo mai visto tanta gente.
rows.en: I'd never seen so many people.

rows.text: Non avevo mai mangiato una pizza così buona.
rows.en: I'd never had such good pizza.

cards.note: Non avevo mai plus a participle says you had never done something before that moment.

cards.headline: Saying nobody did it: nessuno

rows.en: There was nobody at the front desk.

cards.note: Both ways mean the same. At the start, nessuno stands on its own; after the verb, it goes with non before the verb, so the sentence is negative from the beginning.

cards.headline: When nobody got back to you

rows.en: Did anyone get back to you?

rows.text: No, non mi ha risposto nessuno.
rows.en: No, nobody got back to me.

cards.headline: When you're asked if you can manage

rows.text: Ce la fai per le otto?
rows.en: Can you make it by eight?

cards.note: Ce la fai is about making it; me la cavo is about getting by. The little words change with the person: ce la faccio, ce la fai; me la cavo, te la cavi.

cards.headline: When a friend is upset

rows.en: Don't let it get to you, it happens.
Come on, don't let it get to you.

cards.note: Non te la prendere is how you tell a friend not to let something get to them.

cards.headline: Past tense of old stories

rows.en: The square began in the Middle Ages.

rows.text: Il mercante lasciò tutto alla città.
rows.en: The merchant left everything to the town.

cards.note: Nacque, morì and lasciò tell stories about long ago. They mean è nato, è morto and ha lasciato. You only need to recognize them.

cards.headline: When a local tells the history

rows.text: Mio nonno raccontava che la piazza nacque nel Medioevo.
rows.en: My grandfather said the square began in the Middle Ages.

rows.text: Dicono che una famiglia di banchieri rifece tutta la piazza.
rows.en: They say a family of bankers rebuilt the whole square.

rows.text: Ah, quindi la piazza è nata come mercato?
rows.en: Oh, so the square started out as a market?

cards.note: Locals often open a story with "Mio nonno raccontava che" or "Dicono che". Ah, quindi... is a way to check you understood.

cards.headline: When you don't follow

rows.en: What do you mean? Can you explain?

rows.text: Cioè, voglio dire che è stancante.
rows.en: I mean, what I'm saying is it's tiring.

rows.text: Ah, nel senso che non hai tempo?
rows.en: Oh, meaning you don't have time?

cards.note: In che senso? asks the other person to say it another way. Nel senso che lets you check what you think they mean.

cards.headline: Say it another way

rows.text: Cioè, voglio dire che è stancante.
rows.en: I mean, what I'm saying is it's tiring.

rows.text: Mi spiego meglio: sono quattro ore di fila.
rows.en: Let me put it another way: four hours straight.
No, I mean, it's not hard.

cards.note: Cioè, voglio dire, nel senso che and mi spiego meglio all let you say the same thing another way.

cards.headline: When you ask who made it

rows.text: Scusi, quando è stata costruita questa chiesa?
rows.en: Excuse me, when was this church built?

rows.text: E questo affresco, da chi è stato dipinto?
È stato dipinto da un allievo di Giotto.
rows.en: It was painted by one of Giotto's pupils.

cards.note: Use è stata or è stato to match the thing: la chiesa, l'affresco. The painter comes after da, because the line is about the thing, not the person.

cards.headline: About churches
cards.note: In many churches, the lights for the frescoes in side chapels run on coins.

cards.headline: Before: di or che

rows.text: Prima di firmare, vorrei leggere le condizioni.
rows.en: Before I sign, I'd like to read the terms.

rows.text: Prima che tu parta, ti do il mio numero.
rows.en: Before you leave, I'll give you my number.

rows.text: Te la riporto prima che faccia buio.
rows.en: I'll bring it back before it gets dark.

cards.note: When the same person does both things, use prima di plus the -re form. When the other part is about someone else, or the weather, use prima che plus the subjunctive.

cards.headline: Saying it straight out

rows.text: È vero che qui la gente cena tardi.
rows.en: It's true people eat late here.

rows.text: Secondo me è un po' caro.
rows.en: If you ask me, it's a little expensive.
If you ask me, it's closed.

cards.note: So che, è vero che and secondo me present something as a fact or a plain view, so the verb stays as usual: è chiuso, cena.

cards.headline: When you say what you think or hope
cards.note: After penso che, credo che and spero che the verb changes (venga, abbiano, abbia) because it's what you think or hope, not a fact.

cards.headline: When you guess a place is closed
cards.note: Many museums and shops close one day a week, so a guess like this is one you'll make a lot.

cards.headline: When you give a friend advice

rows.text: È importante che tu ti muova ogni giorno.
rows.en: It's important for you to move every day.

rows.text: È meglio che tu non beva caffè la sera.
rows.en: It's better if you don't drink coffee in the evening.

rows.text: Se fossi in te, studierei di più.
rows.en: If I were you, I'd study more.

cards.note: Advice to a friend takes che plus the subjunctive (muova, beva), or se fossi in te plus the 'would' form (studierei).

cards.headline: A set phrase: Se fossi in te

rows.text: Se fossi in te, studierei di più.
rows.en: If I were you, I'd study more.

rows.text: Se fossi in te, chiederei alla padrona di casa.
rows.en: If I were you, I'd ask the landlady.

rows.text: Se fossi in te, cercherei un'altra casa.
rows.en: If I were you, I'd look for another place.

cards.note: Se fossi in te never changes, because you're putting yourself in the other person's place. The 'would' verb that follows is what changes.

cards.headline: Hope or think it already happened

rows.text: Spero che tu abbia dormito bene.
Credo che non abbia ancora letto il messaggio.
rows.en: I don't think he's read the message yet.

cards.note: After spero che, credo che and penso che, something already done takes abbia plus the participle.

cards.headline: When sia needs agreement

rows.text: No, penso che siano già partiti.
rows.en: No, I think they've already left.

rows.text: Spero che il colloquio sia andato bene!
rows.en: I hope the interview went well!

cards.note: With sia, the participle agrees with who or what it's about: arrivata, partiti, andato. It works just like Anna è arrivata.

cards.headline: A small word
cards.note: Che plus a noun, or a describing word and a noun, makes an exclamation. Italian has no word for "a" here: che bella notizia.

cards.headline: As long as: purché

rows.text: Ti presto la bici, purché tu me la riporti stasera.
rows.en: Bike's yours, as long as it's back tonight.

rows.text: Te la presto, purché tu la chiuda col lucchetto.
rows.en: I'll lend it, as long as you lock it up.

rows.text: Va bene, purché tu faccia il pieno prima di riportarla.
rows.en: Okay, as long as you fill the tank first.

cards.note: Purché sets the condition for saying yes. The verb after it is in the subjunctive: riporti, chiuda, faccia.

cards.headline: Unless: a meno che non

rows.text: A meno che non piova, domani andiamo al mare.
rows.en: Unless it rains, we'll go to the beach tomorrow.
Shall we have a picnic in the park?

rows.text: Sì, a meno che non faccia troppo freddo.

cards.note: A meno che non names what would stop the plan. The verb is in the subjunctive: piova, faccia. The non doesn't make it negative.

cards.headline: Feelings: someone else or you

rows.text: Sono contenta che tu sia qui.
rows.en: I'm glad you're here. · che + subjunctive
I'm so glad to see you! · di + verb

rows.text: Mi dispiace di non poter venire.
rows.en: I'm sorry I can't come. · di + verb

cards.note: Use che and the subjunctive for what someone else does, and di and the plain verb for what you do yourself.

cards.headline: When you're glad, sorry or afraid

rows.en: I'm so glad to meet you!

rows.text: Mi dispiace molto che stia male.
rows.en: I'm so sorry he's not well.
I'm afraid of getting it wrong.

cards.headline: When a friend has an exam

rows.text: In bocca al lupo per l'esame!

cards.note: Italians say in bocca al lupo before any exam or interview. The set reply is crepi.

cards.headline: When it's someone's birthday
cards.note: Italians say auguri for birthdays, weddings, births and holidays. The usual reply is grazie.

cards.headline: Likely or only imagined

rows.en: If it rains, I'll stay home. · likely
If it rained, I'd stay home. · only imagined

cards.note: Se plus the present means it may well happen. Se plus the -ssi form, then the 'would' form, means you're only imagining it. Hold the double s.

cards.headline: When you imagine something

rows.text: Cosa faresti se vincessi alla lotteria?
rows.en: What would you do if you won the lottery?

rows.text: Se vincessi, comprerei una casa in campagna con un orto.

cards.headline: About this district
cards.note: Prati means meadows. It was open, flood-prone land by the Tiber until Rome became Italy's capital in 1871. Then it was laid out on a regular grid from the 1880s, so it feels unlike the winding old centre.

cards.headline: About this church
cards.note: The ceiling of Il Gesù, finished in 1679 by Baciccio, mixes stucco figures with painted ones. The eye cannot tell where one ends and the other begins, so the figures seem to tumble out of the frame.

cards.headline: Culture
cards.note: Rome has two big football clubs, Lazio and Roma, and both play at the Stadio Olimpico. Their match is the Derby della Capitale, and families in Rome are often split by it.

cards.headline: About this deli
cards.note: Testaccio grew up around Rome's slaughterhouse. The best beef went to the wealthy, while workers were often paid partly in leftovers: tripe, tail, offal. These are called the quinto quarto, the fifth quarter, and became classic Roman dishes.

cards.headline: About this market
cards.note: Peperoni cruschi are sweet red peppers dried in the sun, a way to keep them through the winter when fresh food was scarce. Fried for seconds in hot oil, they turn crisp and crackle.

cards.headline: Culture
cards.note: Every year a new papier-mâché cart is built for the patron saint's festival. When it reaches the square, the crowd rushes in and tears it to pieces. Everyone wants a piece to take home for good luck.

cards.headline: About this street-food stall
cards.note: Lampredotto is the fourth stomach of the cow, simmered for hours in broth with tomato, onion, celery and parsley. It was working people's food, sold from street carts by the trippai, who used the cheaper cuts nobody else wanted.

cards.headline: Culture
cards.note: Fiorentina fans wear purple, called viola, and no rival is more disliked than Juventus. In 1990 the star player Roberto Baggio was sold to Juventus, and fans rioted in the streets of Florence.

cards.headline: About this church
cards.note: Brunelleschi designed Santo Spirito but died in 1446, before it was built, and work carried on without him. Its facade was never decorated, and still stands smooth and pale above the square.

cards.headline: About this shop
cards.note: The prize of the Palio is not money but the drappellone, a large banner painted anew for every race. An artist is chosen each time, so no two are alike. The winning contrada keeps it in its museum.

cards.headline: About this piazza
cards.note: Palazzo Salimbeni is the seat of Monte dei Paschi di Siena, which began in 1472 as a public fund lending to poor people at fair terms. It is among the oldest banks in the world still operating.

cards.headline: About this restaurant
cards.note: Sarde in saor, fried sardines in a sweet-and-sour mix of onions, vinegar, raisins and pine nuts, began as a way to keep fish for days. It tastes better the day after, so good cooks make it ahead.

cards.headline: About this piazza
cards.note: One statue in Campo dei Mori is known as Sior Rioba. By tradition his nose is made of iron, said to replace a stone nose he lost. Venetians still call the figures by name, like old neighbours.

cards.headline: About this gondola workshop
cards.note: A gondola's hull is deliberately asymmetrical, wider on the left. That way a gondolier rowing from just one side can still move in a straight line. It's built by hand from around 280 pieces of wood.

cards.headline: Culture
cards.note: When Neapolitans are happy about a win, a birth or some luck, they may pay for two coffees and drink one. The second is the caffè sospeso, left for the next person who can't afford it.

cards.headline: About this piazza
cards.note: In Piazza Bellini you can still see stretches of the original Greek walls, made of big tuff blocks, a few metres below street level. Students now sit at café tables over a wall more than 2,000 years old.

cards.headline: Culture
cards.note: Every Neapolitan has a favourite sfogliatella. The riccia has many thin crisp layers shaped like a shell; the frolla is rounder and softer, made of shortcrust pastry. Both are best eaten warm, straight from the oven.

cards.headline: Culture
cards.note: Neapolitans and Romans love to tease each other about pizza. Rome often likes a thin, crisp base; Naples makes it soft and elastic, with an edge that puffs up in the hot oven, a sign of dough that rose slowly.

cards.headline: About this restaurant
cards.note: In Bologna, ragù is served with tagliatelle, never spaghetti. Fresh egg pasta is rough and porous, so its wide ribbons hold the slow-cooked sauce of beef, a little pork, soffritto and a touch of tomato.

cards.headline: About this gelateria
cards.note: Bologna's porticoes began in the Middle Ages, when students needed rooms and buildings extended over the street to make space. Today you can walk the centre in rain or strong sun without an umbrella.

cards.headline: Culture
cards.note: Bologna and Modena have a famous old rivalry. In 1325 Modena won the battle of Zappolino and carried off a wooden bucket from a Bolognese well as a trophy. Modena still keeps it as a symbol.

cards.headline: Culture
cards.note: At a pani ca' meusa stall you must choose: schietta, plain with a squeeze of lemon, or maritata, "married" with ricotta and caciocavallo. People eat it standing, with their hands, and each has a firm opinion.

cards.headline: About this bookshop
cards.note: Il Gattopardo was written by a Palermo aristocrat, Giuseppe Tomasi di Lampedusa. Publishers turned it down, and it came out in 1958, after his death. Its best-known idea: everything must change so that everything can stay the same.

cards.headline: Culture
cards.note: Here it's arancina, feminine, like the orange (arancia) it's named after: round, golden, filled with ragù and peas. On the other side of Sicily it's arancino, cone-shaped like Mount Etna. The argument never ends.

cards.headline: About this osteria
cards.note: An osteria was historically a tavern where people came mainly to drink wine. The host, the oste, served a few simple local dishes from a short menu to go with it. Today many osterie serve full meals.

cards.headline: About this market
cards.note: Slow Food began in Bra, a small Piedmont town near Turin, in the 1980s. It stands for food that is good, clean and fair, and it asks people to eat local food in season.

cards.headline: About this salumeria
cards.note: A food labelled DOP must come from its own area and be made by set rules. Real Parmigiano Reggiano can only come from a small area including Parma, Reggio Emilia, Modena and part of the province of Bologna.

cards.headline: Culture
cards.note: Sunday family gatherings are a custom in Palermo.

cards.headline: About this landmark
cards.note: Every year at Pentecost, at the end of the morning Mass, Rome's firefighters drop thousands of red rose petals through the Pantheon's oculus, for the Holy Spirit coming down.

cards.headline: About this church
cards.note: Baciccio painted the ceiling of Il Gesù in the late 1600s. The figures in the fresco seem to spill out of the frame into the nave.

cards.headline: About this piazza
cards.note: Piazza Navona's long oval follows the shape of the Stadium of Domitian that once stood here. At its centre is Bernini's Fountain of the Four Rivers.

cards.headline: About this church
cards.note: Santa Maria in Trastevere is one of Rome's oldest churches, its apse covered in medieval gold mosaics. Near the altar, fons olei marks where an old story says a spring of oil once flowed.

cards.headline: About this neighbourhood
cards.note: Until Rome became Italy's capital in 1871, Prati was open meadow below Castel Sant'Angelo. The district was built for the new state, with straight streets and squares named after heroes like Cavour.

cards.headline: About this deli
cards.note: Testaccio grew around Rome's slaughterhouse. The cuts its workers took home, the quinto quarto, became coda alla vaccinara, trippa and pajata.

cards.headline: About this osteria
cards.note: Gricia is guanciale and pecorino. Add tomato and it is amatriciana; add egg yolks instead and it is carbonara, never cream.

cards.headline: About this bakery
cards.note: Romans buy pizza bianca and pizza rossa by weight, cut with scissors. They eat it warm on the way to work, sometimes filled with mortadella.

cards.headline: About this restaurant
cards.note: Pane di Matera is made with durum wheat semolina and has its own IGP label.

cards.headline: About this museum
cards.note: This cave house in the Sassi is kept as a family lived in it, with the bed, the loom and the corner for the animals.

cards.headline: About this piazza
cards.note: The Madonna della Bruna is the city's patron saint. On her festa, 2 July, a decorated papier-mâché carriage is pulled through the streets, and the crowd tears it apart at the end.

cards.headline: About this workshop
cards.note: The cucù is a little clay whistle shaped like a rooster. It is a symbol of Matera and a gift for good luck.

cards.headline: About this park
cards.note: The Parco della Murgia Materana is the rocky plateau across the ravine from the Sassi, dotted with cave churches and their old frescoes.

cards.headline: About this bridge
cards.note: The Ponte Vecchio is known as the bridge of the goldsmiths. Jewellers make and repair jewellery in tiny family workshops on it.

cards.headline: About this piazza
cards.note: The Loggia dei Lanzi is an open arcade of statues, free to walk into. Built between 1376 and 1382, it has held Cellini's bronze Perseus since 1554.

cards.headline: About this bar
cards.note: It serves speciality coffee: single-origin beans, roasted lighter, made slowly as an espresso or a filter coffee. It tastes quite different from the usual bar coffee.

cards.headline: About this street-food stall
cards.note: Lampredotto is a bread roll filled with the slow-cooked fourth stomach of the cow, dipped in its broth and topped with green sauce. For locals it's real street food.

cards.headline: About this piazza
cards.note: Every June the Calcio Storico, a rough old football game, is played in this square on sand. A statue of Dante stands in the square.

cards.headline: About this piazza
cards.note: The square is shell-shaped, its paving divided into nine sections. The Palio is run here twice a year, on 2 July and 16 August, on earth laid over the paving.

cards.headline: About this bakery
cards.note: Ricciarelli are soft almond biscuits dusted with icing sugar, and panforte is a dense cake of candied fruit, nuts and spices. Both are Sienese Christmas sweets with medieval roots.

cards.headline: About this osteria
cards.note: Pici are thick hand-rolled spaghetti of flour and water, no egg, typical of Siena. They come with cacio e pepe or with aglione, a big garlic from the Val di Chiana.

cards.headline: About this piazza
cards.note: Palazzo Salimbeni, on this quiet square, is the seat of the Monte dei Paschi bank, among the oldest banks in the world.

cards.headline: About this café
cards.note: Open since 1720 under the arcades of Piazza San Marco. A coffee at a table costs far more than an espresso at the bar, and a music charge is added when the orchestra plays.

cards.headline: About this market
cards.note: Locals shop early at the Rialto market for sarde, seppie and moleche. Moleche are lagoon crabs caught just as they shed their shell, only in certain seasons.

cards.headline: About this square
cards.note: The walls hold statues of merchants in oriental dress, said to be the Mastelli brothers from the Morea. One, Sior Rioba, has an iron nose and counts among the city's 'talking statues'.

cards.headline: About this boatyard
cards.note: The Squero San Trovaso is one of the few boatyards still building and repairing gondolas by hand, from several kinds of wood. The yard looks like a mountain chalet on the canal.

cards.headline: About this bar
cards.note: Naples is where the caffè sospeso began: a coffee paid in advance for a stranger who can't afford one.

cards.headline: About this pizzeria
cards.note: The pizza dough is leavened for many hours, then baked in a wood-fired oven in about a minute.

cards.headline: About this piazza
cards.note: In the middle of Piazza Bellini, parts of the ancient Greek walls of Neapolis show above ground.

cards.headline: About this station
cards.note: The Circumvesuviana to Pompei and Sorrento is run by a separate company, EAV, with its own tickets. Regional paper tickets must be validated at the machines before boarding, or you risk a fine.

cards.headline: About this chocolate shop
cards.note: Gay-Odin has made chocolate by hand in Naples since 1894, and the shop has an art nouveau interior. Its chocolates include the Vesuvio, shaped like the volcano.

cards.headline: About this mozzarella shop
cards.note: Mozzarella di bufala campana is a protected product, made from buffalo milk. It is sold in its own whey and is best when very fresh.

cards.headline: About this street food
cards.note: Pizza a portafoglio is a small margherita or marinara folded in four like a wallet and wrapped in paper. You eat it walking, for a couple of euros.

cards.headline: About this landmark
cards.note: The Portico di San Luca runs almost four kilometres under 666 arches, from Porta Saragozza up to the Madonna di San Luca sanctuary. It is the longest portico in the world.

cards.headline: About this salumeria
cards.note: The Quadrilatero is the old market streets off Piazza Maggiore, where stalls have sold food since the Middle Ages. Mortadella, Bologna's famous cold cut, is sliced to order and sold by weight.

cards.headline: About this church
cards.note: The Bolognese call this group of linked churches and cloisters Sette Chiese, the seven churches, though fewer remain. Its oldest parts are over a thousand years old, and the courtyard holds the Catino di Pilato.

cards.headline: About this restaurant
cards.note: Bologna's classics include tagliatelle al ragù (never spaghetti bolognese), tortellini in brodo, lasagne verdi and cotoletta alla bolognese.

cards.headline: About this pasta shop
cards.note: Sfoglia, the fresh pasta dough, is flour and eggs, about one egg to a hundred grams. It is rolled by hand with a long mattarello until you can see through it.

cards.headline: About this park
cards.note: The giant old Ficus magnolioides trees were brought from Australia in the 19th century. Their aerial roots hang down and spread into trunks, forming shapes like a cave.

cards.headline: About this crossroads
cards.note: This baroque crossroads is at the heart of the old city. Its four corner facades show the four seasons, four Spanish kings and four of the city's patron saints.

cards.headline: About this square
cards.note: The great marble fountain here is nicknamed the Fontana della Vergogna, the fountain of shame, because of its nude statues.

cards.headline: About this chapel
cards.note: This was the royal chapel of the Norman kings. Gold Byzantine mosaics shine under a painted wooden ceiling made by Arab craftsmen.

cards.headline: About this landmark
cards.note: The Pantheon was rebuilt under Emperor Hadrian around 126 AD. Its dome is still the largest unreinforced concrete dome in the world, with an open oculus at the top, so rain falls straight inside.

cards.headline: About this church
cards.note: Il Gesù is the mother church of the Jesuits, finished in the 1500s. Ignatius of Loyola, who founded the order, is buried here in a richly decorated chapel.

cards.headline: About this park
cards.note: Villa Borghese began in the 1600s as the gardens of Cardinal Scipione Borghese. His villa is now the Galleria Borghese, which holds famous sculptures by Bernini.

cards.headline: About this piazza
cards.note: Piazza Navona follows the shape of an ancient Roman stadium built by Emperor Domitian for athletic games. Its long oval is why the square is so unusually shaped. Bernini's Fountain of the Four Rivers stands at its center.

cards.headline: About this church
cards.note: Santa Maria in Trastevere is one of the oldest churches in Rome, with origins in the 200s. The present building dates from the 1100s, and its apse and facade glow with golden mosaics.

cards.headline: About this landmark
cards.note: The Colosseum opened in 80 AD and could hold around 50,000 spectators. Romans came to watch gladiator fights and other public spectacles. It is the largest amphitheater the Romans ever built.

cards.headline: About this museum
cards.note: This cave home is furnished as peasant families lived in the Sassi, often sharing one space with their animals. People lived in these caves until the 1950s, when they were moved to new housing.

cards.headline: About this park
cards.note: Across the ravine from the Sassi, this park protects a rocky plateau full of caves and rock-hewn churches, many with medieval frescoes.

cards.headline: About this piazza
cards.note: Under this square lies the Palombaro Lungo, a huge underground cistern that once stored the town's water. It was forgotten for years and rediscovered in the 1990s.

cards.headline: About this piazza
cards.note: The cathedral on this square dates from the 13th century. It stands on the highest point of the Civita, the ridge between the two Sassi.

cards.headline: About this landmark
cards.note: Butchers once worked in the shops on this bridge. In 1593 Grand Duke Ferdinando I of the Medici replaced them with goldsmiths and jewelers, and jewelry shops still line the Ponte Vecchio today.

cards.headline: About this park
cards.note: The Boboli Gardens lie behind Palazzo Pitti and were laid out for the Medici family from the 1500s. They became a model for the formal gardens of other European courts.

cards.headline: About this piazza
cards.note: Michelangelo's David stood here, at the door of Palazzo Vecchio, from 1504 until 1873. The statue you see there now is a copy; the original is indoors in the Accademia.

cards.headline: About this piazza
cards.note: Every June the square is covered in sand for calcio storico, a rough old Florentine ball game played by teams from the city's historic neighborhoods in costume.

cards.headline: About this park
cards.note: The name comes from the cascine, the dairy farms of the Medici estate that once stood here. The land later became a public park running along the Arno.

cards.headline: About this piazza
cards.note: The square slopes down like a shell, split into nine sections by lines of pale stone. Twice each summer, the Palio horse race is run around its edge on a track of packed earth.

cards.headline: About this piazza
cards.note: The Palazzo Salimbeni, on this square, is the headquarters of Monte dei Paschi, a bank founded in 1472 and often called the oldest bank still operating in the world.

cards.headline: About this market
cards.note: Rialto has been the trading heart of Venice since the Middle Ages. Its fish market still sells the catch of the lagoon and the Adriatic, fresh each morning.

cards.headline: About this landmark
cards.note: Until 1854 this was the only bridge across the Grand Canal. The stone bridge was finished in 1591, and wooden bridges stood here before it.

cards.headline: About this piazza
cards.note: One of the largest squares in Venice, it fills with students in the evening because the university is close by. Cafés and bars spill out across it.

cards.headline: About this market
cards.note: Pignasecca is one of the oldest street markets in the city. Stalls of fish, vegetables, cheese and street food fill its narrow lanes, and locals have shopped here for generations.

cards.headline: About this landmark
cards.note: Castel dell'Ovo stands on a tiny islet in the bay and is the oldest castle in the city. Legend says the poet Virgil hid an egg in its foundations, which gave it its name.

cards.headline: About this piazza
cards.note: In the middle of Piazza Bellini, a sunken excavation shows stretches of the ancient Greek city walls. They are more than 2,000 years old, and you can look down at them from the piazza.

cards.headline: About this landmark
cards.note: Bologna's two medieval towers, Asinelli and Garisenda, date from the 1100s. The Asinelli is about 97 metres tall and you can climb its 498 steps. The shorter Garisenda leans noticeably.

cards.headline: About this church
cards.note: Santo Stefano is not one church but a cluster of linked churches and courtyards, known as the Sette Chiese, the Seven Churches. You walk from one ancient space into the next.

cards.headline: About this piazza
cards.note: Piazza Maggiore is Bologna's main square. The huge Basilica di San Petronio on one side has a front left unfinished: marble covers only the lower part, and plain brick shows above.

cards.headline: About this landmark
cards.note: The Portici di San Luca form the longest covered arcade in the world, about 3.8 kilometres with 666 arches. It climbs from the edge of the city to the Sanctuary of the Madonna di San Luca.

cards.headline: About this landmark
cards.note: The Archiginnasio was the main building of the University of Bologna from 1563 until 1803. Inside is the Anatomical Theatre, a carved wooden lecture hall where anatomy was taught. Today it houses a library.

cards.headline: About this market
cards.note: One of Palermo's oldest street markets, with roots in the Arab period. Vendors call out their goods in loud, singsong Sicilian, a habit known as abbanniare. It's also famous for street food.

cards.headline: About this theatre
cards.note: Teatro Massimo is the largest opera house in Italy, opened in 1897 after more than twenty years of building. Its steps are the setting for the final scene of The Godfather Part III.

cards.headline: About this park
cards.note: Giardino Garibaldi is known for its giant ficus trees. Roots hang down from the branches and grow into thick extra trunks, so each tree looks like a small forest.

cards.headline: About this piazza
cards.note: Its huge fountain was made in Florence in the 1500s and bought by Palermo. Because of its many nude statues, locals nicknamed the square the Piazza della Vergogna, the Square of Shame.

cards.headline: About this piazza
cards.note: Four curved Baroque facades from the early 1600s stand where Palermo's two main streets cross, dividing the old city into four districts. Each facade has a fountain, a season, a Spanish king and a patron saint.

cards.headline: This or that: I'll take it

rows.en: The roll or the little pizza?
The little pizza? I'll take it.

cards.note: Lo stands for a masculine thing and la for a feminine one.

cards.headline: This or that: one day or every week
This or that: asking for some

rows.en: I'd like some bread, said another way.

cards.note: Un po' di is the easy way to say 'some'. Del and della also mean 'some'.

cards.headline: This or that: how long ago
cards.note: Fa after a time means 'ago'. Scorso means 'last'.

cards.headline: This or that: giving your opinion

rows.en: To me, it's good. Same meaning.

cards.headline: This or that: him or her

rows.text: Telefoni a Marco o a Giulia?
rows.en: Are you phoning Marco or Giulia?

cards.headline: This or that: whose is it
cards.note: The answer can use di with a name, or a possessive on its own.

cards.headline: This or that: saying your nationality

rows.en: I'm American, said by a man.
I'm American, said by a woman.

cards.note: Words ending in -e stay the same for both: sono inglese.

cards.headline: This or that: which way to turn

rows.text: Giro a destra o a sinistra?
rows.en: Do I turn right or left?

cards.headline: This or that: at what time
This or that: telling the time
cards.note: One o'clock, noon and midnight take è. Every other hour takes sono le.

cards.headline: This or that: one thing or several

rows.en: Where are the bathrooms? More than one.

cards.headline: This or that: how you get there
cards.note: Transport takes in with no article. On foot is a piedi.

cards.headline: This or that: where you're going
cards.note: Each kind of place has its own little word. Learn them as chunks, like dal medico for the doctor's.

cards.headline: This or that: pointing at it
cards.note: Handy when you don't know the word for it.

cards.headline: Two places: a fried rice ball
cards.note: Both are fried rice balls with a filling. The Roman supplì has tomato rice and a core of mozzarella.

rows.text: A Bologna: le tagliatelle al ragù.

cards.headline: Two places: a street-food sandwich

rows.text: A Firenze: il panino al lampredotto.
A Palermo: il pane con la milza.

cards.note: Lampredotto is cooked tripe, from a cow's fourth stomach. Both sandwiches are sold at street stalls.

cards.headline: Two places: a local sweet
cards.note: Panforte is a dense, spiced cake with nuts and candied fruit. Cassata is a sponge cake with ricotta.

cards.headline: Two places: a long pasta
cards.note: Pici are thick, hand-rolled strands, like fat spaghetti. Tagliatelle are flat ribbons.

cards.headline: Two places: a primo in the north

rows.text: A Venezia: i risi e bisi.
A Bologna: i tortellini in brodo.

cards.note: Risi e bisi is a Venetian dish of rice and peas.
